meta.blurb: Lena Costa has a three-page list and one job: make her best friend's wedding perfect. Then come a storm, a runaway cake, a very bad dog and the best man, Theo Hart. Some things cannot be planned.
meta.bible: Lena Costa: thirty, the maid of honour, an organised events planner from the city who lives by lists; her parents' messy divorce made her distrust big romantic days. Theo Hart: thirty-two, the best man, a quiet ship's engineer who fixes everything and is away at sea for months; Sam's older brother. Ines Duarte: the bride, Lena's best friend since school, warm and nervous. Sam Hart: the groom, Theo's younger brother, sweet and forgetful. Mrs Pruitt: the strict owner of the Saltmarsh Inn, who loves rules and secretly loves weddings. Pudding: Mrs Pruitt's brown spaniel, who steals the rings. Gerald: Theo's old blue van, which breaks down at the worst times. Mr Hollis: a farmer at Hollis Farm, ten miles away, who plays the Accordion; his son Tom plays the Fiddle. Duchess: Mr Hollis's goat, who eats Lena's list. Aunt Dot: Sam and Theo's aunt, who asks too many questions. Vovo Marta: Ines's grandmother, who gives her a blue hairpin. Gull Point: the seaside headland where the wedding is. Saltmarsh Inn: an old inn with crooked floors, a marquee on the lawn and a sea wall. Thursday: arrival and the rehearsal dinner. Friday: the flowers, the cake and the doubts. Saturday: the wedding, in a storm. Sunday: the goodbye. Marquee, Maid, Ring, Rings, Cake, Bouquet, Toast, Vows, Veil, Boatyard, Harbour, Engineer, Platform, Ceremony, Reception, Speech, Tide. Voice and tone: light, funny and warm, a rom-com in which a fussy planner and a calm fixer fall in love over one chaotic weekend; the real ending is on the station platform and a month later; no cruelty, only kind comedy.

Theo said the best weddings are not perfect weddings.

Lena and Theo made the cake look beautiful again.

Lena and Theo ran after the dog along the beach.
They found the dog and the rings, and they laughed.
They ran back, and Lena walked down the aisle with Theo.
Ines and Sam said their promises while the wind blew.

B1B2: Lena Costa sits on the train to the coast with a garment bag on her knees. In her hand is a three-page list, because she is the maid of honour and nothing will go wrong.
The Saltmarsh Inn stands on a windy headland called Gull Point, and its floors are not quite flat. Mrs Pruitt, the owner, gives Lena a heavy key and a page of rules.
In the hall a tall man kneels beside a door with a toolbox. It is Theo Hart, the best man, and he and Lena have met only once, at the engagement party, where they did not get along.
Ines, the bride, is sitting on her bed in a dressing gown when Lena arrives. She says she is excited and terrified, and she asks Lena to keep everything calm.
At the rehearsal dinner the name cards put Lena next to Theo. As maid of honour and best man, they must walk down the aisle together and each give a speech.
The radio says a strong storm will hit the coast on Saturday. Mrs Pruitt says that her marquee has stood in worse, and Theo goes outside to check its ropes.
At midnight Lena cannot sleep and goes down to the kitchen, where Theo is making toast. They argue about whether a wedding needs a list or luck, and then agree to work together for the couple.
On Friday morning the wedding flowers have still not arrived at the inn. Lena rings the florist and learns that the delivery van took them by mistake to Hollis Farm, ten miles away.
Theo offers to drive her in his old blue van, which is named Gerald. Lena says she will come too, because she does not trust anyone else with her flowers.
On the narrow lanes Gerald coughs and Theo talks a little. He is a ship's engineer, he says, and he is often away at sea for four or five months.
At Hollis Farm the flowers are standing in buckets in a cowshed, and Mr Hollis is very sorry. While Lena counts the buckets, his goat Duchess eats a page of her list.
At first Lena wants to shout, but the goat looks so pleased with herself. Lena starts to laugh, and soon she and Theo cannot stop.
On the way back, heavy rain begins to fall, and Gerald slides into a muddy ditch. Lena and Theo get out and push, and by the end they are both covered in mud.
They shelter in a dry barn while they wait for Mr Hollis's tractor. Lena tells Theo that her parents' divorce was so bitter that she trusts lists more than weddings.
Theo listens carefully and then speaks in his slow way. He says the best wedding he ever saw was one where the cake fell on the floor, because everyone remembered laughing.
At last Mr Hollis arrives with his tractor and pulls Gerald out of the mud. They return to the inn at noon, filthy and laughing, with every bucket of flowers safe.
The baker's van arrives with the wedding cake, and the driver looks pale. The road was full of holes, and the top tier has been crushed flat.
Lena wants to cry, but Theo says there is another way. In Mrs Pruitt's kitchen they cut away the crushed part and cover the cake with berries and white roses.
Guests arrive all afternoon, and Lena hands out room keys. Aunt Dot, who is Theo's aunt, asks if the two of them are a couple, and they both say no far too quickly.
On Friday evening Ines and Sam have a silly argument about their first dance. Soon they are shouting about everything, and each wonders if the wedding is a mistake.
Lena finds Ines sitting on the old sea wall in the evening wind. For once Lena does not try to fix anything, and she only listens while Ines cries.
Theo finds his brother Sam at the end of the old pier. Sam says that he is afraid he will not be good enough, and Theo tells him that nobody ever feels ready.
At midnight Lena and Theo meet on the dark stairs, and each tells the other what happened. Theo gives her his jumper, and she feels something warm that is not only the wool.
From a high window Lena and Theo see Ines and Sam on the moonlit beach. The couple talk for a long time, then hold each other, and the argument is over.
On Saturday morning the storm arrives with a roar. Theo and the groomsmen hold the marquee ropes in the wind, while Lena moves the tables into the dining room.
The band calls to say its van has broken down on the coast road. Mr Hollis, who has come to deliver more flowers, says that he and his son can play for the dance.
Lena helps Ines into her wedding dress, and Ines's grandmother Vovo Marta pins a blue clip in her hair. All three of them cry, and Lena has to fix her make-up.
Ten minutes before the ceremony Theo reaches for the rings, but the box is gone. Pudding, Mrs Pruitt's spaniel, has been seen running off with something small.
Pudding races along the wet beach, with Lena and Theo running behind him in their wedding clothes. Lena loses a shoe in the sand, but she does not stop.
At last Pudding stops by a rock and starts to dig. Theo grabs the little box, which is wet but safe, and when he helps Lena up he does not let go of her hand.
Mrs Pruitt has held the ceremony for ten minutes. Lena and Theo hurry in, sandy and breathless, and walk down the aisle together with the ring box in Theo's pocket.
Ines and Sam say their vows in the middle of the storm, and the marquee flaps like a great white sail. The guests laugh at the noise, and Lena cries into her bouquet.
When it is time for the rings, Theo opens the damp little box and hands them over. Sam's fingers shake, and Theo steadies his brother's hands.
At the wedding breakfast Lena stands to give her speech. A gust of wind blows her notes out of the tent, so she puts down the microphone and talks from her heart.
Everyone expects Theo to be dull, but his speech is short, funny and kind. He says that he and the maid of honour have survived a goat, a van and a dog, so marriage should be easy.
Ines and Sam cut the mended cake, and the guests say that it is the most beautiful they have ever seen. Even Mrs Pruitt smiles, and Lena catches Theo's eye.
Mr Hollis and his son strike up a lively tune, and Ines and Sam dance their first dance. Soon the whole room is dancing, and the floor shakes.
Theo walks over and holds out his hand to Lena. She says that dancing is not on her list, and Theo says that it is not on his, either.
As they dance slowly, Lena says she fears that weddings last only one day. Theo says he fears that he is always away, and they admit they like each other.
Late that night the storm finally goes away, and the stars come out over the sea. Lena and Theo slip out of the tent and walk to the stone terrace.
On the terrace Theo turns to her, and for once he does not fix or say anything. He kisses her, softly, and she kisses him back with her whole heart.
After the kiss Theo tells her that he must decide by Monday. A ship wants him for a year, but he has been offered a job at the Gull Point boatyard, and he cannot choose.
At Sunday breakfast Ines sits next to Lena and teases her about Theo. She says that the best parts of her wedding were the parts that went wrong.
In the car park Lena has her bag, and Theo has his hands in his pockets. They say goodbye very politely, and Lena walks to the station alone.
On the station bench Lena takes out a clean page and starts a new list. When the train comes in, she finds that she has written only one word, and she cannot get on.
Back in the car park Theo finds a chewed page under the seat of Gerald. It is the end of Lena's list, and the last line says that she must not fall for the best man.
Theo jumps into Gerald and races for the station. Just before the railway crossing the old engine dies, so he jumps out and runs the last half mile.
Theo races onto the platform and finds Lena sitting alone on a bench. He says that he will take the boatyard job, and she holds up a new list with one word on it, his name.
A month later Lena has arranged to work from the inn two days a week. Mrs Pruitt gives her a key to the room at the top, and the strict old lady almost smiles.
On Friday evening Lena and Theo sit on the sea wall with Pudding and Gerald behind them. She tears her last list into small pieces, lets the wind take them, and kisses him.
C1C2: The train rattled toward the coast while Lena Costa sat very upright, a garment bag across her knees and a three-page list in her hand. Her oldest friend was getting married in three days, Lena was the maid of honour, and she had decided that this wedding would be perfect down to the last napkin. She had never allowed a day to go wrong when she had a list, and she saw no reason to start now.

The Saltmarsh Inn stood alone on the windy headland of Gull Point, its crooked chimneys black against a pink evening sky. Mrs Pruitt, the owner, was a thin woman with a voice like a ruler, and she handed Lena a heavy iron key along with a page of rules that forbade running, candles and dogs in the dining room. Lena loved her at once, because anyone who wrote rules was clearly a kindred spirit.

In the hall a tall man in a faded jumper knelt beside a sticking door with a toolbox open at his knee. Lena recognised him at once as Theo Hart, the groom's brother and the best man, and she remembered that at the engagement party he had said her speech was long enough to need a chair. He looked up, recognised her too, and the polite smile on both their faces did not quite last.

Ines was sitting cross-legged on her bed in a white dressing gown when Lena knocked, and she flew across the room to hug her as though she had been rescued from the sea. She admitted that she was excited and terrified in equal parts, and she begged Lena to make sure that nothing silly went wrong. Lena promised that it would be perfect, in the same steady voice she used on difficult clients.

At the rehearsal dinner the place cards had been arranged by Ines, who was either very innocent or very sly, and they put Lena directly beside Theo. As maid of honour and best man they would walk down the aisle together on Saturday, and each of them would give a speech afterwards. They exchanged one cool glance and then discussed the soup with enormous and very polite interest.

The weather report on the old radio promised a strong storm for Saturday afternoon, just when the ceremony was supposed to begin. Mrs Pruitt waved it away with a thin hand, insisting that her marquee had stood through worse than a little wind, and Theo quietly took a torch and went out to check every rope. Lena ticked one more worry onto the list and told herself that she was entirely calm.

At midnight Lena crept down to the kitchen and found Theo buttering toast at the steel counter, as though he had every right to be there. They argued in whispers about whether a wedding needed a list or a little luck, each convinced the other was wrong, until he pushed a slice across the table. For Ines and Sam's sake, they agreed, they would work together, and for the first time that evening their smiles were real.

On Friday morning the long table in the hall stood bare, and the flowers that should have covered it were nowhere to be seen. Lena telephoned the florist and discovered, with a sinking heart, that the delivery driver had taken the whole order to Hollis Farm, ten miles inland, by mistake. She turned pale, took a breath and reached for her car keys, which she then realised she did not have.

Theo, who had overheard the whole telephone call, offered to drive her to the farm in his old blue van, which he introduced as Gerald. Lena hesitated, since Gerald looked as though he had not passed an inspection since the last century, but she could see no other way to reach the farm. She climbed into the passenger seat clutching her list, and Gerald started on the third try.

Gerald coughed and clattered along the narrow lanes, and in the cramped little cab, with nothing else to do, the two of them began to talk. Theo told her that he worked as an engineer on cargo ships, which kept him away at sea for four or five months at a stretch. He said it lightly, but Lena noticed that he did not say whether he liked it.

Mr Hollis, a red-faced farmer in muddy boots, met them in the yard with a great many apologies and led them to a cowshed full of white roses in buckets. While Lena counted the stems with great seriousness, his goat Duchess wandered up, plucked the middle page of her list from her hand and began to chew it with deep contentment. Lena screamed, Duchess blinked, and Theo made a noise that could only be a laugh.

For one dreadful moment Lena wanted to shout at a goat, and then she looked at Duchess, who stood there chewing with an expression of perfect innocence. A laugh escaped her, then another, and soon she was bent over a bucket of roses wiping her eyes, while Theo leaned against the cowshed wall and laughed just as hard. It was the first time she had laughed properly since the train, and it felt astonishingly good.

They had hardly left the farm when the rain began to fall in great grey sheets, and halfway down a lane Gerald slid gently sideways into a muddy ditch and stopped. Lena and Theo climbed out and pushed from behind with all their strength, slipping, shouting and laughing, until they were brown to the knees and the van had not moved an inch. The flowers sat in the back, perfectly dry and perfectly smug, which seemed deeply unfair.

While they waited in a dry barn for Mr Hollis and his tractor, the conversation turned quieter than before. Lena confessed that her parents' divorce had been so bitter that she had grown up trusting plans more than promises, and that she made other people's weddings perfect because she could not quite believe in her own. She had never said it aloud, and she was surprised that it had been easy.

Theo listened without interrupting, which she had not expected, and then he spoke in his slow, careful way. The best wedding he had ever attended, he said, was one where the cake had fallen on the floor, because ten years later nobody remembered the flowers but everybody remembered laughing. He admitted that he fixed things because he had never learned to say what he felt, and his ears went slightly pink.

At long last Mr Hollis chugged up the lane on his tractor, hooked a chain to Gerald and hauled him out of the mud as easily as a cork from a bottle. They arrived back at the inn at noon, filthy from head to foot, singing something unrecognisable, with every bucket of flowers perfectly safe. Mrs Pruitt looked them up and down and said that there was a hose in the yard.

The baker's van pulled into the car park that afternoon, and the driver climbed out looking pale and miserable. The coast road had been full of potholes, he said, and when he opened the back door the top tier of the wedding cake had slid from its stand and collapsed into a sad, sugary heap. Lena stared at the ruin, and her list, what was left of it, fell out of her hand.

Lena felt tears prickling, but Theo said calmly that cakes could be mended just like engines, and he rolled up his sleeves. In Mrs Pruitt's kitchen they sliced away the crushed part, filled the gaps with cream and then covered the whole thing with fresh berries and the best of the white roses. His hands were surprisingly steady, and when they stepped back, the cake looked far lovelier than the original.

All through the afternoon the guests arrived in noisy waves, and Lena gave out room keys, name tags and directions to the sea. Theo's Aunt Dot, a round and cheerful woman who missed nothing, narrowed her eyes at the pair of them and asked whether they were by any chance a couple. They both answered no at exactly the same moment, a little too loudly, and Aunt Dot smiled to herself and went to find her room.

On Friday evening Ines and Sam began to argue about which song they should have for their first dance, and within five minutes they were shouting about nothing and everything. Each of them said something that sounded like doubt, each stormed off in opposite directions, and the whole inn went silent. Lena, watching from the stairs, felt the floor tilt beneath her as if the whole weekend might collapse.

Lena found Ines on the old sea wall with her knees pulled up and her face wet, staring at the grey waves. Her first instinct was to reach for a list of solutions, but she put it away and simply sat down and listened while her friend poured out her fears. Everyone expected the day to be flawless, Ines whispered, and she was terrified that she would never be able to live up to it.

At the end of the old wooden pier Theo found his brother staring at the water, shoulders hunched against the wind. Sam confessed that he was afraid he would never be good enough for someone as brilliant as Ines, and Theo, who was no good with words, found the right ones anyway. Nobody ever felt ready, he said, and a brother who had spent the whole day arguing about a song clearly cared a great deal.

At midnight they met on the dark staircase, each returning from a different corner of the inn, and sat down side by side to compare their news. Lena shivered, and without a word Theo took off his jumper and put it round her shoulders, and it smelled of salt, wool and engine oil. She noticed that she was not thinking about the list at all, and that it was a very strange thing to notice.

From a window at the top of the stairs, Lena and Theo watched two small figures meet on the moonlit sand far below. Ines and Sam talked for a long time, walking slowly along the edge of the tide, and then they stopped and held each other as though the argument had never happened. Lena let out a breath she had been holding since the evening before, and Theo grinned at her in the dark.

On Saturday morning the storm arrived with a roar, flinging rain against the windows and bending the tall grass flat on the headland. Theo and the groomsmen ran out to hold the marquee ropes while the whole tent bucked like a frightened horse, and Lena, with admirable speed, moved the tables into the dining room as a second plan. She had written the second plan on page two, which was now inside a goat.

A telephone call from the coast road announced that the band's van had broken down and that nobody could say when it would be mended. Lena had just begun to panic when Mr Hollis appeared at the door with a bucket of late flowers, an accordion on his back and his son Tom carrying a fiddle. He had been playing at weddings in the district, he said, since long before Lena was born.

In the bridal room Lena fastened a hundred tiny buttons while Ines trembled with joy and nerves. Her grandmother, Vovo Marta, slipped a small blue hairpin into the bride's dark hair, saying that it had been worn at three weddings and had never failed once. All three women cried at the same moment, and Lena had to repair her make-up with a shaking hand.

Ten minutes before the ceremony Theo reached into his jacket for the ring box and found his pocket empty. A moment later a guest burst in to say that Mrs Pruitt's spaniel, Pudding, had been seen trotting out of the cloakroom with something small and square in his mouth. Theo went white, Lena went white, and they ran for the door at exactly the same time.

Pudding was a small, brown streak racing along the wet sand, and behind him came Lena in her bridesmaid's gown and Theo in a suit that had cost a month's pay. Lena lost a shoe in the first thirty yards, hitched her skirt up to her knees and kept running, shouting the dog's name into the gale. Gulls scattered around them and, high on the headland, a crowd of guests had gathered at the windows to watch.

At last Pudding stopped beside a rock and began to dig with great satisfaction, and Theo dived in and rescued the little box, damp and slightly chewed but with both rings safely inside. They collapsed onto the sand, laughing until neither of them could breathe, and when he pulled her to her feet he kept hold of her hand. Neither of them mentioned it, and neither of them wanted to be the first to let go.

Mrs Pruitt, stern as a general, had held the ceremony for ten minutes by announcing that the music was still being tuned. Lena and Theo slipped into place at the head of the aisle, breathless and covered in sand, and walked down between the rows of smiling guests with the ring box safe in his pocket. Lena had one bare foot and one shoe, and for once she did not care who noticed.

Ines and Sam said their vows beneath a marquee that flapped above them like the sail of a ship, and every time the wind boomed, the guests laughed and the couple smiled harder. Sam's voice shook when he promised to stay with her through every storm, and Ines answered him through happy tears. Lena cried so hard into her bouquet that Theo, beside her, had to hand her a handkerchief.

When the moment came for the rings, Theo opened the damp little box with a face of perfect calm, though his heart was racing, and held it out to his brother. Sam's fingers trembled so badly that the ring nearly fell, and Theo reached out and steadied his hands with his own, quietly, as he had done when they were small. The ring slid on at last, and the whole tent let out its breath together.

At the wedding breakfast Lena rose to give her speech, holding three pages of carefully structured notes, and a sudden gust through the tent flap carried every one of them out over the sea. She stood there for a moment with empty hands, then laughed, and told the room the truth instead: that her best friend had taught her that love was not a plan but a leap. It was the shortest speech she had ever given, and the room rose to its feet.

Everyone expected the quiet engineer to be dull, and he disappointed them gloriously by being funny, brief and unexpectedly moving. He spoke of his brother as a boy who could never keep a secret. Then he added that the maid of honour and he had survived a goat, a muddy lane and a thieving spaniel in one weekend, so marriage should be easy, and his eyes found Lena's across the tent.

Ines and Sam cut the mended cake together while the guests applauded, and a good many of them declared it the loveliest they had ever seen. Even Mrs Pruitt, who was known to have smiled only twice that decade, allowed her mouth to curve upward as the first slice was lifted onto a plate. Lena caught Theo's eye across the table, and they shared a look that no one else in the room could have understood.

Mr Hollis squeezed his accordion into life and Tom joined in on the fiddle, and between them they played a tune so lively that the whole marquee seemed to bounce. Ines and Sam took their first dance, laughing, and within a minute every guest, from the smallest cousin to Vovo Marta, had pushed onto the grass floor. The storm outside was shouting at the canvas, and nobody inside heard a word of it.

Theo crossed the floor, bowed slightly with a face of mock solemnity and held out his hand to Lena. She told him that dancing with the best man was not on her list, and he replied that it was not on his, either, but that lists seemed to have had a bad weekend. She laughed, put her hand in his and followed him into the whirl of the crowd.

They danced slowly, closer than either had intended, while the accordion wheezed a gentle waltz around them. Lena admitted that she had always feared that a wedding was a beautiful day and nothing more, and Theo confessed that he feared he would never be anywhere long enough to deserve anyone. Somewhere in the middle of the confession they stopped pretending that they merely liked each other.

Late that night the storm blew itself out, and the clouds tore open to reveal a sky so full of stars that it seemed unreal. Lena and Theo slipped out of the noisy marquee and walked to the stone terrace, where the wet stones glittered and the air smelled of salt and cut grass. Behind them the fiddle played on, thin and sweet, and neither of them could remember who had suggested the walk.

On the terrace Theo turned to her and, for once in his life, did not try to fix anything or find the right words. He kissed her softly, with the sea breathing below them, and she kissed him back with a force that surprised them both, her hands in his damp collar. It was not on any list, she thought dizzily, and it was absolutely the best thing that had ever happened to her.

After a long silence Theo told her that he had a decision to make by Monday morning. A shipping company wanted him back for a full year at sea, but the boatyard at Gull Point had offered him a post mending boats, near the water and near his brother. Lena said nothing, because she was far too proud and far too frightened to ask him to stay.

At Sunday breakfast, with the guests sleepy and hoarse from dancing, Ines slid onto the bench beside Lena and teased her gently about the best man. She said that the best parts of her wedding had been the broken ones, and that if Lena had made it perfect, she would never have laughed so hard or fallen so well. A list, Ines added with a smile, was a lovely thing, but it had never yet kissed anybody.

In the car park, beside Gerald, Lena stood with her suitcase and Theo stood with his hands thrust in his pockets, and between them lay a whole weekend of things neither of them could say. They said goodbye with the stiff politeness of strangers at a bus stop, and he said that he hoped she would have a good journey. Lena nodded, turned and walked toward the station, and did not trust herself to look back.

On a cold bench at the little station Lena took out a clean sheet of paper and began, out of habit, to write a new list. By the time the train hissed in beside the platform, she had written only a single name, and her legs simply refused to carry her through the doors. The train waited, whistled and rolled away without her, and she sat and looked at the empty track.

Back at the inn, Theo bent to sweep the muddy floor of the van and found a chewed page of Lena's list lying beneath the passenger seat. Most of it was a list of tasks, careful and crossed out, but the last line, written in neat small capitals, read rule seven, do not fall for the best man. He read it three times, began to laugh and then, quite suddenly, did not feel like laughing at all.

Theo flung himself into Gerald and tore toward the station, rattling over every bump in the road. Just before the level crossing the old engine coughed, shuddered and died, and for the first time in his life Theo did not stop to fix it. He abandoned the van in the middle of the lane and ran the last half mile with his heart hammering, his tie flying and his lungs on fire.

Theo burst onto the platform, red-faced and out of breath, and found Lena sitting alone on a bench with an empty suitcase beside her. He told her, between gasps, that he had chosen the boatyard and that he would stay, and she answered by holding up her new list, which bore one word only, his name. He kissed her then and there, while the station cat watched and the ticket collector politely looked at the sky.

A month later Lena had persuaded her office to let her work from Gull Point two days a week, and she set up her laptop at a sunny table in the Saltmarsh Inn with Pudding asleep on her feet. Mrs Pruitt handed her the key to the little room at the top of the house, remarking that it was a good room for a person who did not like to leave, and almost smiled. Lena, who had once believed that she could never trust a place or a person for longer than a weekend, found that she had stopped checking the train times.

On Friday evening Lena and Theo sat on the old sea wall with the sun going down in gold behind them, Pudding snoring beside them and Gerald parked, for once, in the right place. Lena tore her last list into small pieces and let the wind carry them out over the water, where the gulls circled and found them quite uninteresting. Then she kissed the best man, who was the best man in more ways than one, and they went in to dinner, hand in hand, to survive whatever came next.
